strengths: Relevant and well-motivated problem: Directly leveraging Boundary Representation (B-rep) within a unified Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) framework addresses a critical gap in CAD reasoning, moving beyond discrete point clouds and multi-view images.

Principled alignment framework: Employing CoCa-style dual alignment (combining global contrastive loss and autoregressive captioning loss) effectively guides the UV-Net encoder to capture both global topological context and fine-grained geometric details necessary for code generation.

Comprehensive task coverage: Evaluating on reverse engineering, partial completion, error correction, and CAD-QA demonstrates the versatility of mapping geometric B-rep features into structured programming representations.

Thorough discussion of CAD ambiguity: The paper provides insightful qualitative analysis in Section 4.2 explaining why command-level token accuracy (ACC_cmd) does not strictly dictate geometric fidelity (Chamfer Distance), owing to non-unique modeling sequences.
weaknesses: Incomparable and potentially unfair baseline setups in downstream tasks: In Table 2(a) (Completion), BrepCoder is compared against CAD-Llama and general LLMs that only receive ambiguous natural language descriptions, whereas BrepCoder receives full B-rep geometric features. In Table 2(b) (Error Correction), general MLLMs are provided only a single rendered 2D image view, while ReCAD was evaluated on an entirely different dataset and syntax (OpenSCAD). These discrepancies undermine the claims of superiority over baselines.

Questionable and anachronistic citations: Reference [30] cites an alleged 'OpenAI GPT-5 system card. arXiv:2601.03267 (2026)' and reference [8] cites 'Gemini 2.5... arXiv:2507.06261 (2025)', which appear to be non-existent or fabricated citations, compromising the scholarly integrity of the manuscript.

Limited dataset and geometric scope: The evaluation is conducted entirely on DeepCAD (and SGP-Bench for QA). DeepCAD is predominantly limited to sketch-and-extrude operations (essentially 2.5D solids) and does not cover advanced CAD modeling primitives such as sweeps, lofts, fillets, chamfers, or complex freeform B-rep topologies common in industrial CAD.

Missing details on multi-task adaptation: It is unclear whether Stage 2 trains a single unified multi-task model across completion, error correction, and CAD-QA, or if separate task-specific checkpoints are fine-tuned for each downstream application.

Lack of direct comparison with native B-rep LLMs: While BrepLLM (Deng et al.) is discussed in related work, it is not benchmarked against BrepCoder on semantic understanding or CAD-QA tasks where B-rep inputs are utilized.

strengths: Significance of the problem: Directly operating on Boundary Representation (B-rep) as the native CAD format, rather than relying solely on point clouds or 2D renderings, is critical for real-world computer-aided design workflows.

Well-structured framework: Combining a UV-Net B-rep encoder with a CoCa-style pre-alignment (contrastive + captioning loss with attentional pooling) before mapping into an LLM provides a sound and effective multimodal alignment strategy.

Strong reverse engineering performance: On the DeepCAD benchmark, BrepCoder significantly lowers the median Chamfer Distance (0.499 vs. CADCL's 0.972) and achieves an exceptionally low Invalid Ratio (0.009 vs. 13.98%), showing that leveraging pre-trained LLM code generation greatly reduces structural syntax/generation failures.

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper systematically ablates the alignment objective (CoCa vs. CLIP), encoder fine-tuning vs. freezing, model scale, projector depth, and the necessity of Stage 1 reverse engineering pre-training for downstream tasks.

Thoughtful analysis of modeling ambiguity: Section 4.2 and Figure 5 offer a nice discussion explaining why command-level accuracy can be misleadingly penalized despite geometrically equivalent reconstructions.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons in downstream tasks: In the completion task (Table 2a), CAD-Llama and text LLMs receive only an initial code snippet and a vague textual description, whereas BrepCoder receives the complete ground-truth B-rep model (making completion essentially reverse engineering with a known prefix). Similarly, in error correction (Table 2b), baselines receive a single 2D image with inherent scale/occlusion ambiguities, while BrepCoder receives the precise 3D B-rep geometry. These comparisons reflect the superiority of the B-rep modality over text/single-view images rather than an apples-to-apples algorithmic comparison.

Ambiguity regarding multi-task unification: It is unclear whether Stage 2 trains a single unified checkpoint jointly across completion, error correction, and CAD-QA, or if separate models are fine-tuned for each downstream task. Clarifying this is essential to substantiate the claim of a truly unified CAD agent.

Anomalous and questionable citations/baselines: The manuscript includes dubious citations such as reference [30] (OpenAI GPT-5 system card, arXiv:2601.03267) and [8] (Gemini 2.5, arXiv:2507.06261). Evaluating against unreleased/fabricated models undermines the credibility and reproducibility of the experimental reporting.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The individual modules (UV-Net graph encoder, CoCa alignment framework, CAD-Llama code format, MLP projector, and standard instruction tuning) are existing components directly combined for this pipeline.
Formatting neglect: The running head on odd pages persistently reads 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Length', indicating a lack of attention to camera-ready formatting guidelines.

strengths: Directly targeting Boundary Representation (B-rep) for CAD understanding is well-motivated, as B-rep is the industrial standard format containing exact topological and geometric data.
Formulating the CAD generation and editing process as Python-like code (following SPCC conventions) effectively leverages the strong code priors and syntactic reasoning of modern open-source LLMs.

The reverse engineering results on DeepCAD demonstrate a drastically lower Invalid Ratio (IR = 0.009 vs. CADCL's 13.98), highlighting the capability of LLMs to generate syntactically valid and executable CAD programs.

The ablation study thoroughly investigates architectural components, including the contribution of the CoCa alignment loss over CLIP, the necessity of freezing the B-rep encoder, and the effect of model scale.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparisons in downstream tasks: In the code completion task (Table 2a), the proposed method receives the full ground-truth B-rep 3D model alongside partial code, whereas the baseline CAD-Llama is conditioned on ambiguous natural language descriptions. Naturally, having access to the exact 3D geometry provides an overwhelming information advantage, rendering this comparison apples-to-oranges.

Flawed comparative setup for error correction: In Table 2(b), general MLLMs (Gemini, GPT) are evaluated using a single static 2D rendered viewpoint (20° elevation, 45° azimuth), which inherently suffers from occlusion and depth ambiguity, whereas BrepCoder accesses lossless B-rep geometry. Furthermore, the comparison against ReCAD is conducted across completely different datasets and modeling syntaxes (OpenSCAD vs. DeepCAD Python code), which invalidates direct numerical comparison.

Ambiguity regarding the 'unified' multi-task claim: The paper positions BrepCoder as a unified multi-task agent, but Section 4.1 notes that 'Stage 2 data is processed specifically for each task' and the model is fine-tuned across three downstream tasks. It is unclear whether a single multi-task model checkpoint was trained using prompt-based routing or whether separate task-specific checkpoints were trained from Stage 1, which contradicts the core claim of eliminating task-specific models.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed system is largely an integration of existing techniques—combining UV-Net for B-rep graph encoding, CoCa cascaded attentional pooling and dual-loss alignment, the SPCC representation from CAD-Llama, and a standard Qwen2.5 LLM backbone.

Evaluation scope and dataset simplicity: Evaluation is restricted primarily to the DeepCAD dataset, which is limited to relatively simple 2D sketch-and-extrude operations. The evaluation lacks testing on complex industrial CAD operations (e.g., lofts, sweeps, fillets, chamfers) or more diverse benchmarks.

Citation anomalies: The manuscript contains multiple non-standard, questionable, or fabricated citations (e.g., citation [30] citing 'OpenAI GPT-5 system card, arXiv:2601.03267 (2026)' and citation [8] 'Gemini 2.5, arXiv:2507.06261 (2025)'), which undermines the scholarly rigor and credibility of the submission.

strengths: The paper presents BrepCoder, a novel and well-motivated unified Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) architecture that directly takes industry-standard Boundary Representation (B-rep) as input and leverages Python-like CAD code for multi-task CAD reasoning.

The proposed two-phase framework—combining CoCa-style multimodal representation alignment (using both contrastive and captioning losses) with a progressive two-stage LLM training strategy—is technically sound and well-formulated.

Extensive quantitative evaluations demonstrate consistent gains over prior task-specific methods and point/image-based MLLMs across four diverse tasks (reverse engineering, sequence completion, error correction, and CAD-QA), notably reducing the Invalid Ratio to 0.86% and significantly improving geometric Chamfer Distance.

The ablation study is thorough, validating the impact of each major design decision: CoCa alignment vs. CLIP, encoder architecture and freezing, projector design, LLM backbone selection and scale, and the necessity of Stage 1 structural logic pre-training.

The paper provides an insightful analysis of CAD modeling ambiguity (e.g., command order permutations and redundant command elimination), which convincingly accounts for slight discrepancies in token/command accuracy despite superior 3D geometric fidelity.
weaknesses: Evaluation is predominantly centered on the DeepCAD dataset, which primarily consists of basic sketch-and-extrude operations. The framework's ability to handle richer modeling operations (e.g., lofts, sweeps, fillets, complex fillets/chamfers, or multi-body assemblies) remains to be demonstrated.

The multi-task downstream training protocol in Stage 2 lacks full clarity: while framed as a unified multi-task model, Appendix A.2 indicates task-specific hyperparameter configurations (e.g., distinct training epochs and batch sizes for CAD-QA vs. completion/correction), leaving it ambiguous whether a single shared checkpoint serves all downstream tasks simultaneously or if separate fine-tuned models are maintained.

The comparison against large commercial MLLMs (GPT, Gemini) for error correction provides only a single 2D viewpoint to the image baselines; while this underscores the inherent advantage of native B-rep inputs over single-view projections, multi-view renderings would have formed a more competitive and fair baseline for image-based models.

strengths: Formulating B-rep reasoning and manipulation through Python-like procedural CAD code generation allows the model to leverage the rich pre-trained programming and reasoning priors of modern LLMs.

The two-phase, two-stage framework is well-structured: using CoCa-style contrastive plus captioning alignment before projector-based LLM integration ensures feature alignment between complex B-rep face-adjacency graphs and sequential code.

Comprehensive experimental coverage across multiple distinct CAD tasks (reverse engineering, code completion, error correction, and CAD-QA), with solid ablation studies investigating encoder architectures, training stages, LLM sizes, and projector depth.
Insightful analysis of CAD modeling ambiguity (e.g., equivalent geometric solids generated through differing command orders or primitives), supported by qualitative and statistical evidence.
weaknesses: Scholarly rigor and citation integrity concern: Reference [28] cites 'Singh et al.: OpenAI GPT-5 system card. arXiv:2601.03267 (2026)' and reports quantitative benchmarks for 'GPT-5', which appears to be a hallucinated or non-existent citation/model.

Limited dataset diversity and geometric expressiveness: The generative experiments are conducted solely on the DeepCAD dataset, which is restricted to basic sketch-and-extrude primitives. Industrial B-reps frequently require complex operations (e.g., lofts, sweeps, fillets, chamfers, draft angles, complex geometric constraints) that are not evaluated here.

Baseline fairness concerns: Comparing BrepCoder (which consumes full 3D B-rep geometry) against Gemini and GPT fed with a single diagonal 2D rendered image in error correction is inherently unfair, as 2D projections inherently suffer from occlusion and perspective distortion.

Unclear multi-task unification: While presented as a unified general-purpose CAD model, Appendix A.2 indicates that each downstream task in Stage 2 was trained with task-specific hyperparameters and batch configurations, suggesting separate fine-tuned checkpoints rather than a single unified multi-task agent capable of handling all tasks simultaneously without task switching.

strengths: Addressing native B-rep representation within a multimodal LLM framework is timely and practically valuable, as B-rep is the industrial standard format for CAD but has received less attention in MLLMs compared to point clouds and meshes.

The two-phase design—combining CoCa-style pre-alignment (contrastive and captioning objectives between UV-Net B-rep features and Python-like CAD code) with a two-stage LLM training strategy—is principled and well-suited for bridging continuous geometric topology with discrete procedural design logic.

Strong empirical performance: BrepCoder achieves a 52% reduction in Chamfer Distance over prior state-of-the-art (CADCL) and drastically lowers the Invalid Ratio to 0.86% (from >11% in prior work), demonstrating high syntactic and topological validity.

Comprehensive versatility: The model is successfully extended across multiple diverse downstream tasks (reverse engineering, code completion, error correction, and CAD-QA) within a unified architecture, outperforming task-specific and alternative baseline models.

Thorough ablation study and insightful analysis regarding CAD modeling ambiguity (e.g., explaining why ACC_cmd may be lower even when generated geometry is identical or more concise than ground truth).
weaknesses: The evaluation for geometric reconstruction and code manipulation is confined almost exclusively to the DeepCAD dataset. DeepCAD predominantly contains sketch-and-extrude operations (lines, arcs, circles, single extrusions) and lacks more sophisticated CAD operations like lofts, sweeps, fillets, chamfers, or complex multi-body boolean interactions.

Some baseline comparisons are naturally disparate due to modality differences: e.g., commercial LLMs (GPT, Gemini) and ReCAD were evaluated on 2D rendered images because they lack native B-rep support, which puts them at a severe disadvantage for fine-grained coordinate recovery.

Discussion on computational and topological scaling limits is relatively sparse; for instance, how the UV-Net face-adjacency graph and cross-attention tokens scale when handling large industrial CAD assemblies with hundreds of trimmed surfaces.
Reference [28] cites an 'OpenAI GPT-5 system card (2026)', which appears to be a hallucinated or placeholder reference and should be corrected to existing models (e.g., GPT-4o).
